# What is structural interoperability?
## The Problem

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="62%"}
> Can another tool determine **how the dataset is organised** and process it **without bespoke instructions** from the person who created it?
:::

::: {.column width="38%"}
![](images/shared/ash.png){fig-alt="Ash, a researcher" width="70%" fig-align="center"}
:::

:::

## Structural Interoperability 
### Different software tools can reliably understand the organisation of a dataset

- What data objects exist (records, columns, arrays, variables)
- How they are represented (data types, dimensions, coordinates)
- How they relate to one another
- Which values represent missing data
- Whether the dataset follows expected structural rules

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Machines can determine **how** a dataset is organised (structure), even if they do not yet understand **what** the values represent (semantics).
:::

::: notes
Structural interoperability sits between technical and semantic. This definition does not require every explanation to be written inside one file. Meaning may also be expressed through persistent identifiers that resolve to external vocabularies, code lists, specifications, instruments, methods, or provenance records. What matters is that the references and relationships are explicit and machine-actionable rather than hidden in personal knowledge, filenames, or informal documentation.
:::

# How to achieve structural interoperability?
## A shared data contract

A **shared data contract** is an agreement about how data are organised.

. . .

At its centre is the **data model**: the logical structure that software expects to find.

. . .

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
A file extension (`.csv`, `.nc`, `.tif`, `.zarr`) is **not** the contract. It hints at how data are stored, but not how they are organised.
:::

## Choosing a data model

The choice reflects **how you conceptualise the scientific data**. Choose a representation that preserves that structure with the **least** flattening, reconstruction, or artificial complexity.

| I think of my data as… | Natural model |
|---|---|
| "a collection of observations" | Tabular |
| "variables varying along several shared dimensions" | Multidimensional arrays |
| "a collection of meteorological forecast fields" | GRIB |
| "a georeferenced spatial surface" | Raster |
| "geographic objects with properties" | Geospatial features |

::: notes
Example of a dataset: forecast data for 5 variables on 10 pressure levels and 24 time steps. Which model fits best? (Multidimensional arrays, or GRIB if it comes from an operational forecast.)
:::

# Examples of data models and formats

## {background-image="images/structural/data-models.png" background-size="contain" background-color="#ffffff"}

## NetCDF: a data model for multidimensional scientific data

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/structural/netcdf-structure.png){fig-alt="Diagram of a NetCDF file consisting of dimensions, variables, and attributes" fig-align="center"}
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
*Network Common Data Form*: a portable, self-describing format for array data, created at Unidata (UCAR) in the late 1980s.

- **Dimensions:** named axes and their lengths
- **Variables:** typed N-dimensional arrays
- **Attributes:** metadata on a variable or the whole dataset

```text
float air_temperature(time, latitude, longitude)
float surface_pressure(time, latitude, longitude)

air_temperature:units = "K"
```
:::
:::

. . .

Both variables **share dimensions**: the relationship is explicit, not inferred from where values sit in the file.

## What NetCDF does not guarantee

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Dataset A**

```text
float temp(time, latitude, longitude)
temp:units = "K"
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Dataset B**

```text
float T(time, lat, lon)
T:units = "degC"
```
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="NetCDF tells software"}
✔ these are variables<br>
✔ type, dimensions, shape<br>
✔ attributes attached to them
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="It does not tell software"}
? same physical quantity?<br>
? same units?<br>
? are `lat` and `latitude` the same axis?
:::
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**CF Conventions** add the community rules: standard names, units, coordinates, grid mappings:
`temp:standard_name = "air_temperature"`
:::

::: notes

~1-2 min. Ask: can software combine A and B? Structure is fine, but the meaning (and units) differ. Meaning and units are the topic of the semantic interoperability session later in this workshop. Other names for the same quantity that appear in practice: temperature, air_temp, T.
:::


## Exercise: help Ash inspect a NetCDF file {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="70%"}
Ash has received a radar dataset and wants to know **how it is organised before writing any code.**

Open the OPeNDAP page for the IDRA dataset:\
<https://opendap.4tu.nl/thredds/dodsC/IDRA/2019/01/02/IDRA_2019-01-02_12-00_raw_data.nc.html>

Help Ash identify:

1. the global attributes
2. the dimensions and their lengths
3. the coordinate variables
4. three data variables and their dimensions
5. the data types of those variables
6. one variable-level attribute that controls how missing data are represented
7. any variables that hold descriptive metadata as *data values* rather than as global attributes

:::
::: {.column width="30%"}
![](images/shared/ash.png){fig-alt="Ash, a researcher" width="80%" fig-align="center"}
:::
:::

⏱ 10 minutes, in pairs. Do as much as the allows. More: <https://4turesearchdata-carpentries.github.io/interoperability-climate-sciences/structural-interoperability.html>

::: notes
Allow about 10 minutes: pairs need a couple of minutes just to find their way around the OPeNDAP page (look for the Data Descriptor Structure, DDS, and the attributes). The starred items (2, 3, 4, 6) cover the core NetCDF concepts: dimensions, coordinate variables, variables, and the fill value attribute. Items 1, 5 and 7 are extras for faster pairs. Walk around and check that people find the DDS. At about minute 8, check how far people have got, and stop at 10 even if some pairs haven't finished the extras. The solution follows on the next two slides. The point is that Ash can answer all of this from the file itself, without asking its creator.
:::

## Solution: Ash's findings (1/2) {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**1. Global attributes**

`title`, `institution`, `history`, `references`, `Conventions`, `location`, `source`, `example`

`Conventions = "CF-1.4"`: the producer's *intention* to follow CF, not proof of conformance.

**2. Dimensions**

```text
time_raw_data       = 73728
sample_beat_signal  = 1024
time_processed_data = 144
range               = 512
scalar              = 1
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**3. Coordinate variables**

```text
time_raw_data(time_raw_data)
sample_beat_signal(sample_beat_signal)
time_processed_data(time_processed_data)
range(range)
```

`scalar` has no variable of the same name: it is just a length-one dimension used by several variables.
:::
:::

## Solution: Ash's findings (2/2) {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**4 and 5. Data variables, dimensions, types**

```text
i_hh(time_raw_data, sample_beat_signal)
    16-bit integer
equivalent_reflectivity_factor(
    time_processed_data, range)
    32-bit real
radial_velocity(time_processed_data, range)
azimuth_processed_data(time_processed_data)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**6. Missing data**

`_FillValue: -999.0` on `equivalent_reflectivity_factor`, `differential_reflectivity`, `radial_velocity`, `spectrum_width`.

Its existence, location, and type are *structural*. Whether to exclude or interpolate missing values is an *analytical* decision.

**7. Metadata stored as variables**

`iso_dataset`, `product`, `station_details`: string variables, **not** global attributes.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Ash learned all of this from the file itself, with no bespoke instructions: that is structural interoperability at work.
:::

::: notes
Point out that the same structure is visible for any NetCDF file, so Ash's workflow is reusable. Note that `Conventions = CF-1.4` is only a declaration, and that whether the variables are scientifically comparable is a question for the semantic session later. Retrieving the data (OPeNDAP) is covered in the technical session.
:::

## Key takeaways

- Structural interoperability is a **shared, machine-actionable contract** about how data are organised
- A file extension is **not** the contract; the **data model** is
- Choose the representation that matches your **data model**
- NetCDF provides a shared model: **dimensions, variables, attributes**
- **CF** adds the community rules for scientific interpretation

::: notes
Next: semantic interoperability (what do the values mean?) and technical interoperability (how do we retrieve them?).
:::
